newsitem.title: GERMANY: Holzmann to axe up to 10 pct of German workforce.
newsitem.headline: Holzmann to axe up to 10 pct of German workforce.

text.p: Philipp Holzmann AG, Germany's largest building group, said on Wednesday it would shed up to 10 percent of its domestic workforce in 1997 and forecast another operating loss amid a slump in the construction sector.
The builder said it was cutting jobs partly because fierce competition was forcing it to make increased use of subcontractors which paid lower wages.
The cuts would also result from a reorganisation which Holzmann hopes to complete this year. The domestic workforce totalled 24,168 last year. It employed 27,052 people abroad.
Lothar Mayer, chief executive, said the job losses would occur independently of the planned sale in 1997 of shareholdings which now account for 10 percent of construction output.
He painted a dire picture of the domestic building industry this year and predicted Holzmann's new business would decline, while output was likely to stagnate at the 1996 level.

"In Germany construction investment is falling in all areas -- in some parts even drastically. Public sector coffers are empty, industry is moving production abroad, residential construction is shrinking," Mayer said.
He warned that Holzmann may have to draw on company assets again to ensure it breaks even overall. Operating earnings would improve but remain in the red after a loss of 300 million marks in 1996.

In the first five months of 1997 group construction output rose by 8.4 percent to 5.0 billion marks. New business fell by 32 percent to 4.1 billion, largely because orders in the year-earlier period were boosted by several large projects.
Earnings were being hit by losses in the group's project development business and at French subsidiary Nord France and Holzmann's Thai unit.
The company was aiming for another bottom-line break-even in 1997 after a one-million mark net profit in 1996, Mayer said, but added, "We may again have to draw on the company's substance."

"Our principal aim is to return to an operating profit in 1998. We want to be able to pay a dividend as soon as possible." Holzmann has already announced it will omit its dividend for 1997 for the third year running.
The group last year recovered from a 443 million net loss in 1995, but only by realising 1.045 billion marks of group assets and hidden reserves.
The prediction of a narrower 1997 operating loss helped boost the company's share price by 22 marks to 495 marks on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange. The volume of trading was thin.

Mayer also said Holzmann AG and fellow German builder Hochtief AG were determined to press on with their cooperation despite the failure of plans by Hochtief and Deutsche Bank AG to pool their Holzmann stakes which together totalled almost 50 percent.

Deutsche and Hochtief abandoned the pooling plan in June after the European Commission declined to rule on it and said it would refer it to the German Federal Cartel Office, which has already rejected the move.
Mayer said he did not understand the Commission's decision, particularly as it coincided with the merger of French groups Lyonnaise des Eaux and and Compagnie de Suez.
"Nevertheless Hochtief and Philipp Holzmann have decided to work more closely together on the basis of an equal partnership," Mayer said.

Holzmann and Hochtief, which ranked as number 8 and 15 respectively in the world league table, had to keep up with European competitors which were merging to reach the critical mass needed to survive in international markets, Mayer said.
Holzmann was aiming to strengthen its international presence with Hochtief, especially in the U.S. and the growth markets of Asia and South America.
